# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

# Critical Reading of the Two-Year Follow-Up of the Varden Trial and Halden Subset

This is the most useful document in the set. It takes three questions left open by the earlier papers and answers each with a pre-registered analysis:

- **Does the gain last?** Partly. It shrinks but stays above zero.
- **Was the gain entirely an artifact?** No.
- **Do fewer meetings explain part of it?** Yes, in part.

The main conclusions stand. Several details need attention:

- The summary compares two different hours measures, which makes the fall in the gain look larger than it is.
- The mediation test re-examines the same offices that suggested the meetings idea, so it is not an independent replication.
- The meeting audit in two control offices probably biased the 24-month estimate, and the report never says so.
- Backlogs and costs, both raised at nine months, are still not reported for case-processing.

## Arithmetic check

| Item | Check |
|---|---|
| Per hour, timesheets, 24 months | 0.966 / 0.88 = 1.098 → +9.8% ✓ |
| Per hour, system logs, 24 months | 0.966 / 0.89 = 1.085 → +8.5% ✓ |
| Halden subset hours | 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866 → −13.4% ✓ |
| Halden subset per hour | 0.968 / 0.866 = 1.118 → +11.8% ✓ |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 = 100 ✓ |
| Meetings, change in treated minus change in control | (3.9 − 7.4) − (7.0 − 7.2) = −3.3 h/week, matching the nine-month gap ✓ |

Three figures need checking:

- **The summary compares unlike measures.** It reports the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months". The 12.5% is from timesheets and the 8.5% is from system logs. Using timesheets at both points, the fall is **12.5% to 9.8%**, about a fifth. The body of the report makes the correct comparison. The summary overstates the decline.
- **The control offices' meeting average implies something unreported.** Control offices averaged 7.2 to 7.0 hours, a fall of 0.2 hours per office (1.4 hours in total across 7 offices). The two offices that ran the audit fell by 2.1 hours each (4.2 hours in total). For the average to fall only 0.2, the other five control offices must have *increased* their meeting time by about 0.56 hours each. That may be true, but it is not mentioned.
- **The Halden subset baseline matches an earlier figure exactly.** The 11 continuing organisations have a baseline of 40.3 hours. That is identical to the 27-organisation time-tracking average reported by Varga and Holm. It could be a coincidence, but the report should confirm that the baseline is for these 11 organisations.

## Strengths

- **The mediation analysis was registered** at month 11, before the 24-month outcomes were available. It had two named mediators and one outcome.
- **A stricter hours measure was added.** Log-in time on the case system directly addresses the worry about unclaimed overtime raised at nine months. It moved the estimate only slightly, from +9.8% to +8.5%.
- **The decline is reported honestly.** The gain fell by about a fifth on the like-for-like measure. A partial fading of an early effect is plausible, and the report does not hide it.
- **The counter arm's results are reported in full**, including its termination at month 12, the waiting times, and the cost of restoring service (12% more staff, about 9% higher cost per contact).
- **The report clears up the meta-analysis.** It shows that the four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours. That confirms they could not test whether effects decay.
- **The caveats are appropriate.** The Halden survivors are described as "survivors twice over". The meeting audit is described as uncontrolled, with only two offices. The report also correctly says that no arm reorganised work without cutting hours.

## Problems

### 1. The mediation test is the same data, not a replication
The meetings hypothesis came from these seven treated offices at month six. The registered test, filed at month 11, re-examines those **same seven offices**, and their meetings had already been cut by month six (to 3.8 hours, and 3.9 at month 24).

Registration protects against choosing the analysis after seeing the results. It does not turn the test into independent confirmation. The summary's word "confirms" is too strong. "Survives a registered test" is the accurate phrasing.

Two further points:

- **Sample size.** The claim of "a larger sample of office-months" overstates the information available. Meeting cuts vary between offices, so the effective sample for the mediator is still 7 treated against 7 control offices. With so few clusters, a confidence interval as narrow as 28–66% is probably too tight, the same problem I raised with the nine-month standard errors.
- **Order of mediators.** Fewer meetings could themselves reduce fatigue. If so, how the 65% explained is split between the two mediators depends on the order in which they are modelled. The report does not say how that was handled.

### 2. Where did the baseline for meeting time come from?
The nine-month report said meeting data were collected only in month six. This report gives baseline figures of 7.4 hours for treated offices and 7.2 for control. Those were probably recovered from calendar history after the fact. If so, the report should say so, and should say whether recurring meetings were identified the same way in both periods.

### 3. Log-in time may not fit the meetings mechanism
The definition matters. Log-in time "records time staff are working on cases", so it may capture only case work.

If so, cutting meetings would mainly move time *into* case work. That would raise output per **total** hour, but would not obviously raise output per **case-work** hour. Yet the registered outcome is output per log-measured hour. Fewer meetings could still help through less fragmented, more focused work, but that is a different mechanism from reclaiming time, and it should be stated.

If instead the logs record total log-in time, including time spent in meetings while logged in, they are a different measure from the one described. Either way, the report needs to define it precisely.

There is a related question. Logs were added at follow-up, so a difference-in-differences estimate needs pre-period log data. Was it extracted after the fact?

### 4. The control-office meeting audit probably biases the estimate toward zero
Two of the seven control offices cut their meetings at month 15 and gained about 4.1% in output per hour. That raises the control group's average by roughly **1.2 percentage points** (4.1% × 2/7) during months 15 to 24.

As a result, the 24-month treatment effect is **understated**, and some of the apparent decline from 12.5% to 9.8% may come from the control group improving rather than the treatment effect fading. The report presents the audit as evidence about mechanism, but never notes this effect on its main estimate. A sensitivity analysis leaving out those two offices should be reported.

The 4.1% figure itself is a comparison of each office with its own previous six months. It does not account for seasonality and was not compared with the other control offices.

### 5. The registered primary outcome is understated
The registered primary outcome is **output per FTE**. It moved from −2.1% to **−3.4% (CI −8.0% to +1.2%)**, drifting downward, and a loss of up to 8% cannot be ruled out. The summary and Section 5 lead with the per-hour result, which is a secondary outcome. For an employer deciding policy, the per-employee figure is the one that matters, and "mostly, not fully, offset" is the right description of it.

### 6. Two items from the nine-month report are still missing
- **Backlogs and statutory deadline breaches.** The nine-month report itself named these as a concern. Two years of system data should show them.
- **Cost per case closed.** Overtime was claimed throughout. The county costed the counter arm (about +9% per contact) but did not do the same for case-processing. That asymmetry is unexplained.

### 7. The Halden subset

- **Response rate.** Only 14 of the 23 organisations responded. The 9 non-responders could include more organisations that reverted.
- **Timing of reversions.** The Halden paper reported three retail and hospitality organisations reverting at the *end of the pilot*. It is unclear whether the two retail and hospitality reversions here are those same organisations or new reversions after the pilot. The marketing agency is new. The distinction matters for how stable the arrangement proves over time.
- **Two years without a comparison group.** General productivity change over 2023 to 2025, including new tools, is mixed into the +11.8%. "Upper bound" is a fair label in spirit, but strictly this is an unadjusted estimate, not a bound.
- **The attrition question is not addressed.** Okafor, the lead author of the Halden pilot, co-authored this report. It does not respond to Varga and Holm's finding that Halden's withdrawals happened after the schedule began, not during preparation as the original paper said.

### 8. The authors are partly assessing disputes about their own work
The report evaluates criticisms of the authors' own earlier papers. That does not invalidate it, since the key analyses were registered. But it is a reason to want the mediation result tested in an independent setting.

## Where the five documents leave things

| Question | Best current answer |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain in work that can be queued, with strict measurement | **About 8–10%** at two years. The randomised Varden estimate is +8.5% on logs and +9.8% on timesheets. |
| Is it entirely an artifact? | **No.** The Varden estimate meets every standard Varga and Holm recommended. |
| Does it last? | **Partly.** It fell by about a fifth from 9 to 24 months, and contamination of the control group may account for some of that fall. There is only one controlled study with long follow-up. |
| Output per employee in work that can be queued | **About −2% to −4%.** Mostly offset, not fully, and the trend is slightly downward. |
| Work that depends on staff being present | **Fails without extra staff.** The county ended the counter arm. Restoring service required about 12% more staff and about 9% higher cost per contact. |
| Mechanism | **Meetings matter and fatigue matters less.** The test was registered but used the same offices that generated the hypothesis, so it needs replication elsewhere. About a third of the gain is unexplained. |
| Can the gain be captured without cutting hours? | **Open.** Two control offices suggest partly, but the design needed is an arm that reorganises work without reducing hours, and no study has run one. |

The debate has settled close to the meta-analysis's adjusted figure. The most important remaining question is the last one in the table. If cutting meetings delivers much of the gain without reducing hours, the case for a shorter week would rest mainly on wellbeing and retention, not productivity.
